title: Design a metrics and logging pipeline
summary: Telemetry from 20,000 hosts: agents, a stream in the middle, processing, a time-series store and cheap log storage; cardinality explosions, downsampling, retention, and why percentiles cannot be averaged.

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
body: **The ask:** every service in the company sends metrics and logs. Engineers build dashboards and alerts on the
metrics and search the logs during incidents.
| Kind | Requirement |
| Functional | ingest metrics (counters, gauges, histograms) and logs; query by labels and time; alert rules |
| Non-functional | alerts evaluate on data under a minute old; the pipeline must **not** fall over during an incident (when everyone queries and every service logs errors); cost per GB matters |
| Out of scope | distributed tracing storage (same pattern, mention it), the dashboard UI |
```text
hosts      20,000, each exposing ~1,000 active series
series     20 M active series
samples    20 M / 15 s scrape interval ≈ 1.3 M samples / s
storage    ~1.5-2 bytes / sample after compression ≈ 2-2.7 MB/s ≈ 170-230 GB / day
logs       20,000 hosts x 50 lines/s x 300 bytes = 300 MB/s raw ≈ 26 TB / day
Metrics are cheap **per sample** but expensive **per series**. Logs are cheap to write but huge. Both shape
the design.

steps.prompt: How many samples per second does the metrics store ingest? (Integer division.)
steps.explain: Every series produces one sample per scrape. Halving the scrape interval to 7.5 s doubles this, and so does doubling the series count: series count is the number to watch.

steps.title: The pipeline
body: ```text
hosts: app --> agent (e.g. OpenTelemetry Collector, Fluent Bit)
| batches, retries, buffers to disk
v
[ log / stream: Kafka topics, partitioned by source ]      <-- absorbs spikes, replayable
stream processing              log indexer
(aggregate, drop labels,         |
compute rollups)                v
|                 hot index (days) --> object storage (months, cheap)
v
time-series store (raw 15 s for 15 days, 5 min rollups for 1 year)
alerting rules + dashboards
- The **stream in the middle** decouples producers from storage: if the store is slow, data waits in Kafka
instead of being dropped by 20,000 agents at once.
- **Pull vs push:** Prometheus-style scraping pulls from targets (the server controls the rate and knows when a
target is down); push (OTLP) suits short-lived jobs and many network setups. Large systems use both.
- **Downsampling and retention tiers** keep a year of history at a fraction of the cost: nobody needs 15-second
points from last March.

prompt: **Symptom first.** After Tuesday's deploy, the metrics store's memory went from 40 GB to 310 GB and queries time
out. `promtool tsdb analyze` on a block shows:
What happened and what is the fix?
options: A label with unbounded values (session_id) turned one metric into millions of series. Drop the label (relabel it away) and put per-session detail in logs or traces
Traffic grew 8 times overnight: scale the metrics store
The scrape interval is too short: change 15 s to 60 s
Compression is broken in this block: delete it
steps.explain: Every distinct combination of label values is a new series with its own memory and index entries. Ids (users, sessions, requests, full URLs) never belong in metric labels. Slower scraping would cut samples, not series.

steps.title: Cardinality, downsampling and retention
body: **Series for one metric = the product of its label value counts.**
```text
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket
route (200) x method (4) x status_code (8) x le buckets (12) x pods (300)
= 23 M series      <- already too many: drop pod, or aggregate before storing
- Keep labels **bounded**: route templates (`/orders/{id}`) not raw paths, status classes, regions.
- **Aggregate early** in the stream processor (sum over pods) when nobody queries per pod.
- **Downsample** old data: keep min, max, sum and count per 5 minutes, which still gives averages and peaks.
- **Logs** go to a hot index for a few days, then compressed files in object storage that can still be
queried (slowly). Sampling debug logs is fine; dropping error logs is not.

steps.title: You cannot average percentiles
body: Host A serves 1,000 requests a second with p99 = 0.5 s. Host B serves 10 a second with p99 = 2.5 s. The fleet
p99 is **not** (0.5 + 2.5) / 2 = 1.5 s. Percentiles are positions in a sorted list; averaging them ignores how
many requests each host served and how they were spread.
**Histograms can be merged.** Each host counts requests per latency bucket. Bucket counts simply add up across
hosts, and the percentile is then read from the merged counts:
```text
host B             0      0      1       2    4     3
p99 = the bucket where the running total reaches 0.99 x 1,010 = 999.9  ->  <= 0.5 s
In PromQL: `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))`. Prometheus
buckets are cumulative (`le` = less than or equal) and it interpolates inside the bucket; the idea is the same.

steps.prompt: Two services report their own p99 latency to your dashboard: 120 ms (9,000 requests/s) and 800 ms (100 requests/s). What is the p99 across both?
options: It cannot be worked out from the two p99s; you need their histograms (bucket counts) to merge
steps.explain: Even a weighted average of percentiles is wrong: the combined p99 depends on the whole shape of both distributions. Export histograms (or a mergeable sketch) and compute the quantile after summing.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: metrics and pipeline
steps.body: What you reach for when dashboards lie, the store runs out of memory or telemetry arrives late.

toolkit.what: Computes a percentile from summed histogram buckets: the correct way to get a fleet-wide p99.
flags: add buckets across instances, keep the bucket label
per-second rates over a window, robust to counter resets
toolkit.when: every latency SLO panel and alert

toolkit.what: Counts active series per metric name, to find which metric exploded.
Reads a Prometheus data block and lists the labels and metrics with the most series and label values.
flags: optional: one block instead of the newest

toolkit.what: Validates alerting and recording rule files before you deploy them.
flags: unit tests for rules with fixed input series
toolkit.example: promtool check rules alerts/slo.yml && promtool test rules tests/slo_test.yml
toolkit.when: in CI for every rule change

toolkit.what: Shows how far the pipeline's consumers are behind the stream, per partition: late telemetry starts here.
flags: the consumer group, e.g. the indexer
toolkit.when: logs or metrics show up minutes late

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the question it answers.
pairs: What is the p99 across the whole fleet?
Which metrics have the most series?
Which label has the most distinct values?
Does this alert fire on the data I expect?
How far behind is the indexer?

steps.title: Merge histograms, then take the percentile
prompt: Write `double Percentile(double[] upperBounds, long[][] hostCounts, double q)`:
- `upperBounds` are the buckets' upper bounds, ascending. Each `hostCounts[h]` has one count **per bucket** (not
- Sum the hosts' counts bucket by bucket, then return the upper bound of the first bucket where the running total
- `q` outside `(0, 1]` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`; no requests at all throws
starter: double Percentile(double[] upperBounds, long[][] hostCounts, double q)
solution: double Percentile(double[] upperBounds, long[][] hostCounts, double q)
for (var i = 0; i < merged.Length; i++) merged[i] += host[i];
hints: First add the hosts' arrays element by element into one `long[]`.
Then walk the buckets with a running total and stop when it is at least `q * total`.
template: Dojo.Eq("fleet p99 from merged buckets", 0.5, Percentile(dojoB, new[] { dojoA, dojoSlow }, 0.99));
Dojo.Eq("the slow host alone has a p99 of 2.5 s", 2.5, Percentile(dojoB, new[] { dojoSlow }, 0.99));
Dojo.Eq("so averaging the p99s (1.5 s) would be wrong: fleet p99 is not 1.5", true, Percentile(dojoB, new[] { dojoA, dojoSlow }, 0.99) != 1.5);
Dojo.Eq("fleet p50", 0.05, Percentile(dojoB, new[] { dojoA, dojoSlow }, 0.5));
Dojo.Eq("fleet p99.9 reaches the slow tail", 2.5, Percentile(dojoB, new[] { dojoA, dojoSlow }, 0.999));
Dojo.Eq("q = 1 is the last non-empty bucket", 1.0, Percentile(dojoB, new[] { dojoA }, 1.0));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("q must be above 0", () => Percentile(dojoB, new[] { dojoA }, 0));
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("no requests at all", () => Percentile(dojoB, new[] { new long[6] }, 0.5));
